title: The poem and its date
short: Idea 61, Drayton's best-known sonnet, first appeared in the 1619 folio of his Poems, a quarter-century after the sequence began.
body: Drayton's sonnet sequence first came out as Ideas Mirrour (1594) and was reprinted and heavily revised many times; this sonnet is not in the early versions. Martha Foote Crow's edition, based on the 1619 text, states that the famous sixty-first appears for the first time in 1619, so it is the work of a poet in his fifties looking back on the Petrarchan mode rather than a young sonneteer's exercise. The title 'Idea' is Platonic (the ideal form of the beloved); the sequence is often linked to Anne Goodere, daughter of Drayton's patron, but this poem names no one. The archive keeps the old spelling of the 1619 print, with u for v and v for u ('helpe', 'vs', 'haue') and capitalised key nouns. Claims online that the sonnet dates from 1594 confuse the sequence with the poem.

sources.cite: Martha Foote Crow, ed., Elizabethan Sonnet Cycles: Idea, Fidessa, Chloris (1896), introduction and text of Idea LXI
Michael Drayton, Poems (London, 1619), Idea, sonnet 61 (copy-text of Crow's edition)

anchor: Come let vs kisse and part
title: kiss and part
short: A brisk, colloquial opening: the kiss is a formal leave-taking, not a lover's caress.
body: The line sounds like ordinary speech; there is none of the elaborate address that opens most Elizabethan sonnets. A parting kiss was a customary farewell gesture, and here it seals what the speaker presents as a mutual and final settlement. The monosyllables and the strong pause after 'helpe' give the line the tone of someone cutting short an argument. Readers have long admired the way the octave mimics brusque, manly resolve, while the extra emphasis ('yea glad', l. 3) quietly gives that resolve away: a man who protests that he is glad is perhaps not glad. The whole first eight lines work as a performance of indifference that the last six undo.

title: Nay, I have done
short: Dramatic phrasing: the speaker answers an unheard reply, as if the woman had objected or asked for more.
body: 'Nay' implies an interlocutor: the poem reads like one side of a conversation already in progress. 'I have done' means 'I have finished (with this, with you)', and 'You get no more of Me' reverses the usual sonnet situation, in which the lover begs for favours; here he refuses to give any more of himself. This dramatic, speaking voice is often compared with Donne's lyrics and with Shakespeare's late sonnets, and it is one reason the poem has seemed modern to many readers.

title: glad with all my heart
short: The insistent repetition of 'glad' hints that the speaker's relief is protested too much; the tone of the octave is open to question.
body: 'Withall' is the 1619 spelling of 'with all'. The doubled 'glad' can be taken straight (the speaker really is relieved to be free) or as overemphasis that betrays the opposite feeling. Most modern readers take the second view, because the plea of the couplet shows that the freedom of line 4 ('so cleanly, I my Selfe can free') was never wanted. 'Cleanly' means neatly, without mess or residue, and perhaps also with a clear conscience. The tension between bluff octave and pleading sestet is the poem's main effect.

title: Shake hands ... cancel all our vows
short: Legal and business language: shaking hands closes a deal, and to cancel is to annul a written bond.
body: To 'shake hands for ever' is to part on agreed terms, as partners do when dissolving a contract. 'Cancel' comes from Latin cancelli, the lattice of crossed lines drawn through a deed to void it, so the lovers' vows are imagined as documents struck through. The language treats love as a mutual covenant that can be ended by consent, which makes the mythologised deathbed of the sestet all the more striking: what the octave treats as a cancelled contract, the sestet treats as a dying person.

title: Be it not seen ... in either of our brows
short: 'Scene' is the archive's spelling for 'seen' (1619 'seene'); the lovers must show no trace of old love on their faces.
body: The archive text reads 'scene', apparently a transcription slip for 'seene', the 1619 spelling of 'seen'; the sense is 'let it not be seen'. The brow was the conventional place where feeling could be read in a face (compare 'the brow of care'). The speaker is planning their public behaviour: when they meet again, neither should betray 'one jot' of the former love. The concern with appearances suits the poem's social, almost legal framing of the separation.

title: one jot
short: 'Iot' is 'jot', the smallest particle, from the Greek letter iota; the phrase echoes Matthew 5:18.
body: Old printing did not distinguish i and j, so 'iot' is 'jot'. The word comes through Latin from Greek iota, the smallest letter of the alphabet, and the idiom was made familiar by Christ's saying that not 'one jot or one tittle' of the law shall pass away. The speaker's claim that no jot of love remains is therefore a claim to complete erasure, which the sestet will reverse.

title: The turn (line 9)
short: The volta: after an English-style octave of two quatrains, line 9 turns from brusque farewell to an allegory of Love dying.
body: Drayton uses the English (Shakespearean) rhyme scheme, three quatrains and a couplet, but the thought divides like an Italian sonnet, eight lines and six. 'Now' at line 9 marks the shift in tone from the plain speech of the octave to an elevated, slow, ceremonial allegory. A second 'Now' at line 13 marks a further turn, so the poem effectively has two voltas, the last one giving the couplet its reversal. The doubled superlative 'last gaspe of Loues latest Breath' slows the line with heavy stresses, imitating laboured breathing.

sources.cite: Martha Foote Crow, ed., Elizabethan Sonnet Cycles: Idea, Fidessa, Chloris (1896), introduction and text of Idea LXI

title: The deathbed of Love
short: Love is personified as a dying man attended by Passion, Faith and Innocence, like figures in a morality play.
body: The sestet stages a deathbed scene. Love's pulse is failing; Passion lies speechless; Faith kneels in prayer by the bed; Innocence performs the last office of closing the dead man's eyes. These personified abstractions recall the allegorical figures of the morality plays and of emblem books, and they give the private quarrel the dignity of a ritual. Each figure fits the dying relationship: the passion has gone dumb, fidelity can only pray, and innocence presides over the end. Critics often note that the shift from colloquial speech to allegory is itself the argument: the speaker's language rises, betraying how much the love still means.

anchor: when all haue giuen him ouer
title: given him over
short: 'Given over' is the medical term for a patient the physicians have abandoned as past cure.
body: To 'give over' a patient was to stop treating him because death was certain. The phrase continues the deathbed metaphor: everyone, Passion, Faith and Innocence included, has given up on Love. 'Would'st' (wouldst) makes the woman the only possible physician. Note the feminine rhymes 'ouer / recouer' (over / recover), whose falling extra syllable gives the closing couplet a soft, imploring cadence after the hard monosyllables of the opening.

anchor: From Death to Life, thou might'st
title: The final couplet
short: The couplet reverses the octave: the speaker who announced a clean break now begs the woman to revive the love.
body: 'From death to life' has a religious ring (a resurrection, a miracle of revival), and only the woman can perform it. The reversal invites different readings: a sincere change of heart forced by the allegory the speaker himself has conjured; a tactical manoeuvre, in which the show of indifference was always a lover's ploy to provoke a response; or a poised irony in which the speaker knows that both moods are true. The conditional 'if thou would'st' leaves the outcome open. Many anthologists have counted it among the best sonnets of the age precisely because so much is compressed into this last turn.
